(Today through Friday)...
Issued at 312 AM EDT Sat Aug 15 2026

Through 7AM: 

Rapid convective development is occurring upstream from central 
Illinois westward along and north of a quasi-stationary front at the 
nose of a 30-40KT southwesterly low level jet. This activity will 
expand and push eastward through daybreak, likely making it into 
northwestern portions of the forecast area. Modest effective shear 
values and weak mid-level lapse rates suggest very limited severe 
potential.

The atmosphere across the region remains deeply and anomalously 
moist, however, with precipitable water values near the top end of 
the climatological envelope. Highly efficient rainfall rates 
continue to be a concern, owing to this deep moisture, and deep warm 
rain processes, as freezing levels remain at or above 15,000 feet. 
Needless to say, much of central Indiana, particularly central and 
northern portions of the area, remains waterlogged tonight, and any 
additional convective rainfall will rapidly pose a flash flood 
threat.

7AM through Noon: 

The aforementioned convection will continue to push across the area 
through the morning hours, with CAMs suggesting the northern half to 
two thirds of central Indiana likely to see additional 
storms/rainfall. Primary concerns will be heavy rain and isolated 
strong to damaging wind gusts, but due to strong low level shear an 
isolated tornado cannot be ruled out entirely.

Noon through Saturday night:

Additional diabatic pressure losses over northern Indiana throughout 
the day will continue an MCV with a SE progression this afternoon. 
This will likely lead to additional convection NE of the I-74 
corridor with isolated damaging wind gusts possible once again. 
Given the orientation of this newly formed MCV to the low level jet, 
training thunderstorms will be possible with a moderate (level 3 of 
4) risk for excessive rainfall. This area will have very low flash 
flood guidance values due to prior rainfall and therefore flash 
flooding will likely have an extremely rapid onset. There is some 
uncertainty with the specific placement of the precipitation axis 
with the afternoon rainfall, with the best case scenario keeping the 
precipitation axis north and east of the highly vulnerable region - 
recent high resolution model runs are somewhat less promising in 
this regard, however.

Once the MCV exits the region, height rises once again should limit 
convection, keeping any rainfall mostly as a light shower during the 
Saturday evening hours. That said, the heavy rainfall threat will 
sadly not be over, as the nocturnal LLJ is expected to ramp up again 
late Saturday night with moderate isentropic lift and additional 
scattered to numerous convective showers and thunderstorms. 

In additional to the rainfall mentioned earlier, southerly winds 
will bump temperatures up over the south and southwest portions of 
the state, especially where cloud cover will be less abundant. This 
is expected to create a window of 100-106 heat index values Saturday 
and Sunday afternoon along and south of a line from Sullivan to 
Bloomington to Seymour and thus a Heat Advisory has been issued for 
this area from 11AM today until 8PM Sunday.

Sunday and Sunday Night...

Northwest flow aloft will continue into the latter portion of the 
weekend, with one or more upper level disturbances passing through 
the area bringing continued threats for thunderstorms and heavy 
rainfall. Extension of the ongoing flood watch into Sunday may 
eventually be needed but will forgo this for now with the pressing 
concern of ongoing threats and potential additional flash flooding 
today at top of mind.

Instability will again be very strong in an extremely moist airmass, 
though deep layer shear will be more modest. The gradual passage of 
a cold front during the mid to late day hours along with enhancement 
from any additional potential MCVs will serve to focus possible 
severe potential along with additional heavy rainfall and flash 
flooding threats. The primary severe threat would be damaging winds, 
though again an isolated tornado cannot be entirely ruled out. The 
more significant and pressing threat will remain flash flooding 
given the extreme amounts of rainfall this week and extreme 
sensitivity to additional high rainfall rates with convection.

Monday and Tuesday...

An area of surface high pressure will mercifully bring at least a 
temporary end to the repeated rounds of thunderstorms early in the 
week, with dry weather and near normal temperatures likely early 
Monday into late Tuesday.

Wednesday...

Unfortunately, an additional round of thunderstorms appears likely 
Wednesday into Wednesday night as another cold front and upper level 
wave accompanying a strong jet streak aloft passes through the 
region. Plentiful moisture will be available, though precipitable
